sentences.text: Alamosaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore and the only described North American titanosaur from the Late Cretaceous.
Its anatomy featured a small head supported by a long, robust neck, a broad and bulky torso, cylindrical legs for weight support, and a tail slightly smaller relative to the rest of the body.
The parent group of Alamosaurus is Saltasaurinae, a classification that explains its robust anatomy and forelimbs positioned higher than its hindlimbs.
Fossils found near the K/T boundary make Alamosaurus one of the last recorded titanosaurians before the mass extinction event.
Alamosaurus is known for having multiple specimens preserved in various states of completeness, which is uncommon for large titanosaurians.
Thomas Holtz proposed that the largest adults could have reached over 30 meters in length and weighed between 72.5 and 80 tonnes or more.
Exceptional fragmentary remains found in Chihuahua, Mexico, include a broken tibia estimated at 165 cm long, attributed to Alamosaurus.
The genus and species were named by Smithsonian paleontologist Charles W. Gilmore in 1922.
The holotype of Alamosaurus was discovered in June 1921 by Gilmore, Reeside, and Sternberg in New Mexico.
Definitive fossils of Alamosaurus sanjuanensis come from the Ojo Alamo Formation.
The most complete known specimen is a recently discovered juvenile skeleton in Texas, which allowed for accurate estimates of length and mass.
Trackway evidence indicates Alamosaurus walked slowly at 3.2 to 4 km/h without dragging its tail.
Studies estimate Alamosaurus growth lines formed between 4 and 12 years, with a maximum lifespan of 55 years.
The association of Alamosaurus and Quetzalcoatlus likely inhabited semi-arid inland plains.
Fossils of Alamosaurus from the Evanston Formation in Wyoming indicate it shared its environment with Triceratops.
Friedrich von Huene classified Alamosaurus within the family Titanosauridae in 1927.
Alamosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago during the late Maastrichtian stage.
Alamosaurus fossils are found in what is now southwestern North America, where it became the dominant large herbivore in southern Laramidia.
Alamosaurus is one of the few sauropods known to have lived in North America after a 30-million-year gap in the fossil record.
It is debated whether fossils from formations like the North Horn, Black Peaks, and Javelina belong to Alamosaurus or a distinct genus.
Scientists debate whether a massive tibia found in the North Horn Formation belongs to Alamosaurus or a new sauropod species.
A third hypothesis proposes that Alamosaurus originated in Asia rather than South America.
Researchers suggest Alamosaurus likely migrated to North America from either South America or Asia.
